model.comments: High effort Claude Fable 5.1. Thinking is always on for Fable; depth is controlled by Anthropic's output_config.effort, which OpenRouter sets from reasoning.effort (its verbosity field maps to the same native field, so this equals the older opus-4.x verbosity convention).

prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Chess (move selection from provided legal moves). - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(pieces: dict[str, str], to_play: str) -> str: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player whose turn it is (given by `to_play`). - `pieces` is a dictionary mapping squares to piece codes, e.g. `{'e1': 'bK', 'f3': 'wR'}`. - Squares are in algebraic coordinates: file `a`-`h` and rank `1`-`8` (e.g. `'e4'`). - Piece codes are two characters: color + piece type. - Colors: `'w'` = White, `'b'` = Black. - Piece types: `K` King, `Q` Queen, `R` Rook, `B` Bishop, `N` Knight, `P` Pawn. - `to_play` is either `'white'` or `'black'`. - For example: pieces: {'f1': 'wK', 'd1': 'bK', 'a4': 'wN', 'h3': 'wP', 'a5': 'wP', 'h4': 'bP'}, to_play = 'white' - You are not allowed to import the `chess` module. You are allowed to import other python modules or numpy. # Action / Return Format - Return exactly ONE move string that is an element of `legal_moves`. - Do not return any extra text, commentary, or formatting—only the move string. - The move strings is a UCI move string and almost always 4 characters long. Examples: `'b4b5', 'g3e1', etc. Castling is simply represented as a king move (e1g1, e1c1, e8g8, e8c8) - The only time the move strings is longer than 4 characters is when a pawn promotion is involved. Examples: 'a2a1r', 'a2a1b', 'a2a1n', 'a2a1q' moves the pawn from a2 to a1 and promotes it to one of four piece types.The move strings does not include any extra characters for captures, checks, or disambiguation. - Example format of `legal_moves` you might receive: - `['f5e4', 'f5f4', 'g3d6', 'g3e1', 'g3e5', 'g3f2', 'g3f4', 'g3h2', ...]` - Your goal is to choose the strongest move under standard chess objectives: prioritize checkmate if available; otherwise prioritize winning material, improving king safety, and preventing immediate threats. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I need to write a chess policy function with signature policy(pieces, to_play), meaning I have to generate legal moves myself without the chess module. Since I don't have castling rights or en passant info, the safest approach is to skip castling entirely to avoid risking an illegal move that could disqualify the solution.

For efficiency under a 1-second time limit, I'll use pure Python with a mailbox board representation, alpha-beta search with iterative deepening, quiescence search, MVV-LVA ordering, and piece-square tables, generating pseudo-legal moves and filtering for king safety. As long as my move set is a subset of the engine's legal moves (no castling, no en passant), this stays safe.

I'm planning the piece encoding scheme and move generation using precomputed attack tables for knights, kings, and sliding pieces, plus check detection via reverse attack lookups. For evaluation I'll use material plus simplified piece-square tables, and for search I'm setting up negamax alpha-beta with iterative deepening, time checks, quiescence search on captures, and move ordering via a transposition table.

I'm weighing whether Zobrist hashing is worth the incremental overhead versus simpler killer-move/MVV-LVA ordering, and leaning toward implementing incremental Zobrist hashing since it shouldn't be too costly and improves move ordering. My priority is correctness first—no illegal moves, no crashes, respecting time control—then strength, with a time budget around 0.6s using node-count checks and falling back to the previous completed iteration's best move if a deeper iteration gets aborted mid-search.

I'm making sure depth 1 always completes by capping quiescence search depth and checking time within quiescence itself, with fallbacks to a partially-searched best move or a simple capture-first ordering if nothing else is available. Since I don't have move history, repetition detection isn't feasible, but I'll handle mate/stalemate scoring correctly, returning a mate score adjusted by ply when there's no legal move and in check, or zero for stalemate.

Now I'm setting up piece values and square indexing, then precomputing knight, king, and sliding-piece ray attack tables. Writing move generation logic...

For unmaking, I restore the piece and captured piece back to their original squares, and I'll track king positions separately as variables rather than scanning the board each time for speed. For evaluation, I'm setting up piece-square tables using the standard Simplified Evaluation Function, converting the conventional rank-8-first layout into my own indexing scheme with separate white and black tables. I'm planning to maintain the material and PST score incrementally during make/unmake rather than recomputing from scratch, adjusting the score by removing the old piece-square value and adding the new one whenever a piece moves or is captured.

I'll handle king position specially by computing its PST contribution only at evaluation time based on game phase (middlegame vs endgame), rather than incrementally, since that requires just two lookups. I'm also considering adding endgame-specific bonuses like driving the enemy king toward the edge when they only have a king left, plus a small tempo bonus, while skipping mobility and passed-pawn bonuses to keep things fast.

Now I'm outlining the alpha-beta search itself: for each depth, it probes the transposition table, generates and orders moves, makes each move while filtering out illegal ones that leave the king in check, recurses negamax-style, updates alpha/beta and the best move, and handles checkmate/stalemate when no legal moves exist. I'm also adding check extensions -- increasing depth by one when in check -- while thinking through how to avoid infinite extension loops from perpetual check sequences, reasoning that each extension is balanced out since both the checking move and the response consume a ply.

I'm designing the quiescence search to only explore captures and promotions past the main search depth, using a stand-pat evaluation as a lower bound and delta pruning to skip captures that can't possibly raise alpha, plus a hard depth cap to prevent runaway recursion. For move ordering, I'm setting up a scoring scheme that prioritizes the transposition table move, then MVV-LVA for captures, promotions, killer moves, and finally history heuristic values. I'm also sketching out the Zobrist hashing scheme with random keys per piece-square combination and side-to-move, updated incrementally, feeding into a transposition table dictionary with size limits.

For performance, I'm thinking about minimizing Python's attribute-lookup overhead by binding board state to local variables inside hot loops, and structuring the root search to generate legal moves, short-circuit if there's only one legal move, and otherwise run iterative deepening with periodic time checks against a roughly 0.6 second budget to leave safety margin for slower machines.

I'm also handling edge cases: guaranteeing depth 1 always completes, and building a fallback for the rare case where legal move generation misses something like en passant, since castling-only situations can't actually occur. The fallback tries an en passant capture guess, then any pseudo-legal move, then a dummy move as a last resort.

Now I'm setting up the core engine constants, square conversion helpers, and precomputed move tables for knights and kings, along with sliding-piece ray directions, then defining piece-square tables for evaluation starting with pawns.

Adding piece-square tables...

Since castling isn't allowed here, the king middlegame table's reward for g1 is mostly moot, though it might still nudge the king to walk over manually via f1, which costs tempo but isn't harmful.

For piece encoding I'm mapping each piece type to an index (1-6 for white, 7-12 for black), then building a combined piece-square table that folds material value and positional bonus together per square, with kings handled separately since their scoring depends on game phase. I'm keeping an incremental score updated during moves, plus tracking non-pawn material to determine phase, and blending king middlegame/endgame tables based on that phase, with special handling for lone-king endings.

I'm defining a mop-up evaluation term that pushes the losing king toward the edge and the winning king closer, triggered when material is decisively imbalanced and non-pawn material is low, to help drive checkmates like KQ vs K.

Now I'm starting to write the actual search engine class, beginning with its constructor.

Setting up state fields...

I'm designing the make-move function that updates the board, incremental score, hash, and material counts, plus an undo stack storing the previous state for rollback.

Writing unmake and attacked-square logic...

I'm double-checking the pawn attack direction math for both colors, then moving to move generation: I'll only promote to queen and knight to cut down the branching factor, since underpromotion rarely changes outcomes.

Writing move ordering logic...

Setting up the search function with transposition table lookups...

Finishing the alpha-beta loop with killer/history heuristics on cutoffs, handling mate/stalemate detection, and storing the TT entry with the correct bound flag. I'm double-checking king-safety lookups use the mover's side before the flip, noting mate scores stored relative to ply are slightly imprecise but tolerable, and considering adding null-move pruning for extra speed.

I want to guard null move against zugzwang in low-material endgames, but I'm worried about a subtle bug: our move generator allows pseudo-captures of the king, which only get filtered out by the legality check on the actual mover, and null move might let that check slip through incorrectly since we're skipping our own move.

Since we only make a null move when we're not in check, the opponent can't ever end up capturing our king afterward, and quiescence search has the same legality guarantees, so king captures genuinely never occur in either search path. For quiescence itself, I'm writing the standing-pat evaluation, delta pruning against captures, and the alpha-beta cutoff loop over ordered capture moves.

For the root search, I'm structuring an iterative deepening loop that tracks a deadline, falls back to the previous best move on timeout, and returns immediately if there's only one legal move. Within each depth iteration, I want partial results preserved -- so if a timeout interrupts a move's search, I fall back to whatever move already completed at that depth rather than an incomplete one.

I'm reasoning that with fail-soft negamax and best-first ordering, any later move beating alpha at the root gets an exact score since beta stays at infinity, so keeping that partial best is theoretically sound. I'll skip aspiration windows for now and cap max depth around 20, relying on the time budget to limit actual search depth given Python's likely node throughput.

I'm settling on roughly a 0.6-second time budget checked every few hundred nodes, using a fixed-seed Zobrist hash for reproducibility, and keeping the transposition table scoped per call rather than persisting it globally to avoid memory growth. Now I'm writing the evaluation function that pulls in material score and non-pawn material to decide endgame-specific king safety logic.

Writing endgame king evaluation...

I'm noting the mop-up bonus should distinguish winning vs losing king, using center distance and king distance tables to push the weaker king toward the edge. I also want to make sure the parsing step converts the incoming pieces dictionary and side-to-move correctly, and wrap the top-level policy logic in a try/except so any failure falls back to returning a safe legal move.

For the fallback path, I'm planning to compute legal moves independently of the search so if the search throws an exception I can just grab the first legal move, preferring captures, or fall back to a pseudo-legal guess if the legal list ends up empty. The move string just needs the origin square, destination square, and promotion letter when relevant.

Now I'm setting up precomputed knight, king, and sliding-piece move tables indexed by square to speed up move generation, binding local variables instead of repeated attribute lookups for performance. Writing move generation tables...

I'm also building piece-square tables for evaluation (converting rank-8-first tables into indexed arrays for both colors), setting up material values per piece type, and initializing Zobrist hashing keys for board state plus side-to-move, then computing the initial position's score, material count, hash, and king squares during setup. Writing zobrist and PST setup...

Now I'm writing the pseudo-legal move generator, iterating over squares to filter for the side's own pieces, then handling pawn moves including single/double pushes, promotions, and preparing to add diagonal capture logic.

Continuing with knight/king moves using precomputed offset tables and slider pieces using ray-based movement with directional break-on-capture logic, plus setting up slide direction constants for bishops, rooks, and queens. I'm also starting to sketch null-move pruning conditions in the search function, checking depth, ply, and material thresholds before allowing a null move.

I want to flag whether consecutive null moves should be permitted, adding a null_ok parameter to control that. I'm also considering a cautious late-move reduction scheme for quiet moves beyond the fourth in the list at sufficient depth, doing a reduced-depth search first and re-searching at full depth if it beats alpha, since that's a reliable standard gain. For move ordering at the root, I'll rely on transposition table hits, the previous iteration's best move, and MVV heuristics, which should be sufficient without overcomplicating things.

Now I'm sketching the top-level policy function: it converts the piece dictionary into a board array, determines side to move by checking if the string starts with 'w', builds an Engine instance, and grabs legal moves — falling back immediately if none exist or returning the single move if only one is available. Otherwise it calls the engine's think function with a time budget, wrapping it in a try/except so any failure defaults to the first ordered legal move, and wraps the entire outer logic in another try/except that returns a safe fallback move string if board parsing itself fails. I'm now working out the edge case where no legal moves are found except a potential en passant capture, checking if one of our pawns sits on the fifth rank next to an enemy pawn with an empty square diagonally ahead.

I also need to handle piece code parsing for strings like 'wK', map them to numeric values, and guard against a missing king breaking the attack-detection function by wrapping that logic in a try block too. I'm adding a periodic time check inside the search loop that raises a timeout once the deadline passes, and reasoning through how check extensions interact with quiescence search — making sure a position in check always gets a one-ply extension so evasions get evaluated, while bounding this extension by ply depth and also capping overall search ply to avoid runaway recursion. Finally, I want the evaluation function itself to be lightweight and fast.

Now I'm working out the mop-up evaluation for king-and-rook-vs-king endgames, building distance tables between squares and to the center to bias the score toward driving the enemy king to the edge and closer to material. I verify the legality check after making a move by re-checking whether the mover's king is attacked using its updated position, and I set up killer-move and history tables alongside a transposition table for move ordering.

Writing engine class code...

Working through move ordering: transposition-table moves get top priority, then captures scored by victim value minus attacker value, then promotions, then killer moves, then history heuristic scores, with everything sorted descending before being searched.

I'm adding late-move-reduction logic that reduces search depth for quiet, non-check, later-ordered moves and re-searches at full depth if they unexpectedly raise alpha, while keeping in mind that check extensions still apply on top of this.

Writing root search loop...

I'm structuring the iterative-deepening root search so it keeps track of the best move found so far, catches timeouts by falling back to the last complete result, and breaks early if a forced mate score is found — while being careful that raising a timeout mid-recursion could leave the board in a modified state, so I decide it's safe to just abandon the engine entirely on timeout rather than trying to unwind moves.

I'm also thinking about repetition avoidance: since this position evaluator gets reused across moves in the same game, I want to track visited position hashes globally and treat repeated positions as drawish (score zero) when searching deeper than the root, so the engine avoids repeating positions when it's ahead materially. I add a heuristic to detect if it's actually a fresh game (all 32 pieces present, pawns on starting ranks) to reset this repetition memory, and cap the memory size to avoid unbounded growth.

Writing Zobrist and distance tables...

I'm also reasoning through quiescence search's delta pruning, skipping obviously hopeless captures unless there's a promotion involved, and reconfirming that a king can never legally be captured in this framework so I don't need special-case handling for that during move generation.

Writing legal move generation...

For detecting en passant when no other legal move seems to exist, I reason that if castling and every other move are impossible, the only legal move left must be the en passant capture, so I just pick whichever candidate en passant square applies without needing to disambiguate further, since the game state guarantees a legal move must exist.

Writing engine helper methods...
